pos: n. pl. (great rolling waves; breakers — Hebrew mishbar, a breaker)
etymology: Old Norse bylgja, a wave. The Hebrew mishbar comes from the root to break — a billow is a wave at the moment it breaks over a man.
biblical_def: Billows are breaking waves, and both places where the Authorized Version uses the word are prayers out of the depths, and both call the waves God's own. The sons of Korah: “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” (Psa 42:7). Jonah, from the fish's belly: “For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me” (Jon 2:3). The possessive is the whole doctrine. Not the billows but thy billows — the affliction is not loose in the world; it belongs to God and is under His hand. Jonah goes further and says God cast him there, which is exactly true: the sailors threw him overboard, and Jonah credits the throwing to the LORD. That is not resignation, and it is not fatalism. It is the ground of the prayer, because a man whose trouble is an accident has no one to pray to about it, and a man whose trouble is from God's hand has. So Jonah prays, and reports the answer in the same chapter: “I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice” (Jon 2:2). The psalm answers itself in the same way: “Yet the LORD will command his lovingkindness in the daytime, and in the night his song shall be with me” (Psa 42:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a billow as a great wave or surge of the sea, occasioned usually by violent wind; a wave swelled and driven.
webster_full: BIL'LOW, n. A great wave or surge of the sea, occasioned usually by violent wind.
BIL'LOWY, a. Swelling or swelled into large waves; full of billows or surges.
SURGE, n. A large wave or billow; a great rolling swell of water.
WAVE, n. A moving swell or volume of water; a billow.
scriptures: Psalm 42:7
Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me.
Jonah 2:3
For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me.
Jonah 2:2
And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice.
Psalm 42:8
Yet the LORD will command his lovingkindness in the daytime, and in the night his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life.
corruption_summary: Affliction is assigned to chance, to the devil, or to nobody, and the sufferer is left with a trouble that has no author and therefore no address for prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: Both passages say thy billows, and everything hangs on the pronoun. Modern comfort works the other way: it assures the sufferer that God had nothing to do with it, hoping to protect His character. The comfort is short-lived, because a wave that God did not send is a wave He is not governing, and a man under it has nothing to pray about except that the weather improve. Jonah, who had every reason to plead accident, says God cast him into the deep — and immediately prays, because the hand that cast him was the only hand that could lift him out.

This must not be flattened into fatalism, which Scripture does not teach. Jonah was in the sea for his disobedience and says so; Psalm 42 is written by a man pouring out his soul and questioning why he is cast down. Neither writer is calm. What both do is keep the affliction attached to God rather than let it float free, and out of that attachment comes prayer, and out of the prayer comes the answer both record. The believer who says thy billows has already conceded the hardest point and gained the only thing worth having in deep water.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishbar (H4867), a breaker, billow — Psalm 42:7, Jonah 2:3, Psalm 88:7, 2 Samuel 22:5; from shabar (H7665), to break.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishbar (H4867) — a breaker or billow; Psalm 42:7, Jonah 2:3, Psalm 88:7, 2 Samuel 22:5.
Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break in pieces; the root, so a billow is named for what it does when it lands.
Hebrew gal (H1530) — a wave; the companion word in both passages.
Hebrew tehom (H8415) — the deep; Psalm 42:7, deep calling unto deep.
Both occurrences are in prayers, and both call the waves God's own.
usage: “All thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” — the pronoun is the doctrine.
“Thou hadst cast me into the deep” — said by the man the sailors threw.
“I cried… and he heard me” — the answer recorded in the same chapter.

pos: n. pl. (clefts; fissures in rock — Hebrew seiph and chagav)
etymology: An older English form of clefts, from cleave, to split. The word names a split in rock, whether used as a shelter, a hiding place, or a shrine.
biblical_def: Clifts are clefts in the rock, and Scripture puts three very different things in them. They shelter the destitute: Job describes men driven out from among their fellows “to dwell in the clifts of the valleys, in caves of the earth, and in the rocks” (Job 30:6). They housed idolatry at its worst: Isaiah charges Judah with “enflaming yourselves with idols under every green tree, slaying the children in the valleys under the clifts of the rocks” (Isa 57:5) — child sacrifice practised in the rock hollows of the wadis. And in the terrible day men will run into them: “To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks, for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth” (Isa 2:21). Against all three stands the one cleft that saves. Moses asked to see God's glory, and was answered: “while my glory passeth by, that I will put thee in a clift of the rock, and will cover thee with my hand while I pass by” (Exo 33:22). A man cannot see God and live; therefore God provides both the cleft and the covering hand, and the glory passes. Rocks hide men from God in judgment; one Rock hides a man in the very presence of God and he lives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cleft as a space or opening made by splitting; a crack; a crevice; and clift as an obsolete or dialectal form of the same word.
webster_full: CLEFT, n. A space or opening made by splitting; a crack; a crevice; as the cleft of a rock.
CLIFT, n. The same as cleft; a fissure or opening in a rock; used in the Scriptures.
CLEAVE, v.i. To part or divide by natural separation; to split.
ROCK, n. A large mass of stony matter; figuratively, defense; means of safety; protection.
scriptures: Isaiah 57:5
Enflaming yourselves with idols under every green tree, slaying the children in the valleys under the clifts of the rocks?
Job 30:6
To dwell in the clifts of the valleys, in caves of the earth, and in the rocks.
Exodus 33:22
And it shall come to pass, while my glory passeth by, that I will put thee in a clift of the rock, and will cover thee with my hand while I pass by:
Isaiah 2:21
To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks, for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth.
corruption_summary: Child sacrifice is treated as an extinct barbarism of the ancient world, and the God whose glory Moses could not survive is reduced to a manageable friend.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 57:5 describes the slaying of children in the valleys under the clifts of the rocks, and the practice is regularly filed away as an atrocity of the vanished past. It was not exotic even then: it was carried out by the covenant people, in their own land, alongside a temple where the true sacrifices were still being offered, and it was defended by the religion of the day. Every age finds a way to spend its children for its own advantage and to name the spending something else. The prophets did not treat it as a lapse but as the logical end of idolatry, since a false god always finally asks for what is dearest.

Exodus 33:22 rebukes the opposite corruption, which is the domestication of God. Moses — who spoke with God face to face as a man speaks to his friend — asked to see His glory and was told that no man can see His face and live. The provision was a cleft in the rock and a covering hand, and even then only the back parts were shown. Where God is preached as immediately accessible on any terms a man likes, this chapter is unintelligible, and so is the cross, since the cleft and the covering hand are what a mediator is. Isaiah 2:21 shows the alternative: men who would not be hidden in the Rock will be calling on the rocks to hide them.
roots_summary: Hebrew seiph (H5585), a cleft of a rock — Isaiah 57:5; nikrah (H5366), a fissure — Exodus 33:22; chagav (H2288), a crevice — Obadiah 3, Song of Solomon 2:14.
roots_lines: Hebrew seiph (H5585) — a cleft or fissure of rock; Isaiah 57:5, Judges 15:8.
Hebrew nikrah (H5366) — a cleft; Exodus 33:22, its only occurrence, of the cleft that held Moses.
Hebrew chagav (H2288) — a crevice, refuge in rock; Song of Solomon 2:14, Jeremiah 49:16, Obadiah 3.
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — a rock; the standing figure for God as the refuge of His people.

usage: “Slaying the children… under the clifts of the rocks” — done by the covenant people.
“I will put thee in a clift of the rock, and will cover thee with my hand”.
Rocks hide men from God; one Rock hides a man before Him.

pos: n. pl. (dense undergrowth; a place of hiding — Hebrew sebak and choresh)
etymology: From thick, Old English thicce. The Hebrew sebak is an interwoven tangle of branches — the same word used of the thicket that held the ram at Moriah.
biblical_def: Thickets in Scripture are where men go when they are afraid. Under Philistine pressure, “the people did hide themselves in caves, and in thickets, and in rocks, and in high places, and in pits” (1Sa 13:6). Jeremiah sees the same flight in Judah's last days: “The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks: every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein” (Jer 4:29). But the thicket is no shelter when God is the pursuer. Isaiah makes it fuel: “For wickedness burneth as the fire: it shall devour the briers and thorns, and shall kindle in the thickets of the forest, and they shall mount up like the lifting up of smoke” (Isa 9:18); and the standing forest of Assyrian pride is felled: “he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one” (Isa 10:34). The tangle that hides a fugitive from an army burns in a moment and falls to an axe. Behind all of it stands the first thicket in Scripture, on Moriah, where a ram was caught by his horns in a thicket and died in the place of Isaac — the one thicket in the Bible that ever saved anybody, and it did so by yielding up a substitute.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a thicket as a wood or collection of trees or shrubs closely set; a close cluster of underwood or brushwood.
webster_full: THICK'ET, n. A wood or collection of trees, shrubs, etc., closely set; as a ram caught in a thicket.
THICK, a. Dense; close; crowded; not thin or scattered.
BRAKE, n. A place overgrown with brakes or brambles; a thicket.
COV'ERT, n. A shelter; a defense; a thicket or shady place affording shelter.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 13:6
When the men of Israel saw that they were in a strait, (for the people were distressed,) then the people did hide themselves in caves, and in thickets, and in rocks, and in high places, and in pits.
Jeremiah 4:29
The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks: every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein.
Isaiah 9:18
For wickedness burneth as the fire: it shall devour the briers and thorns, and shall kindle in the thickets of the forest, and they shall mount up like the lifting up of smoke.
Isaiah 10:34
And he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one.
corruption_summary: Men look for cover from consequences rather than for a covering from God, and every hiding place in Scripture fails except the one that holds a substitute.
corruption_paragraphs: Hiding is the oldest instinct after sin: Adam went among the trees of the garden, Israel went into the thickets, and Judah climbed the rocks. In every case the cover is real against men and useless against God, who asked in Eden the question that ends all such attempts — where art thou? Isaiah's picture is deliberately terrible: the very tangle men run into becomes the fire's fuel and goes up like smoke. Whatever a man puts between himself and the judgment of God — distance, respectability, busyness, doctrine held without obedience — belongs to the same class of shelter.

Genesis 22 is the exception that makes sense of the rest. Abraham lifted up his eyes and behind him was a ram caught in a thicket by his horns, and he offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son. That thicket held a substitute, and the mountain was named the LORD will provide. This is the pattern for the whole Bible. There is no hiding place that answers the judgment of God except the one in which a substitute is caught and offered, and the substitute finally provided on that same range of hills was His own Son.

Hebrew ab (H5645) — a thicket, and also a cloud; Jeremiah 4:29.

“It shall kindle in the thickets of the forest” — the cover becomes the fuel.
The one saving thicket held a ram, and the mount was named the LORD will provide.

pos: n. pl. (the beds of watercourses; the deep courses of the sea — Hebrew aphiq)
etymology: Latin canalis, a pipe or groove, through Old French chanel. The Hebrew aphiq means a containing channel — the bed that holds a stream, and by extension anything strong and confining.
biblical_def: Channels are the beds of waters, and Scripture shows them laid bare by the breath of God. David's song of deliverance: “the channels of the sea appeared, the foundations of the world were discovered, at the rebuking of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils” (2Sa 22:16); the psalm repeats it: “Then the channels of waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were discovered at thy rebuke, O LORD, at the blast of the breath of thy nostrils” (Psa 18:15). The picture is of the sea driven back to its floor by a word, as at the Red Sea. What a man cannot see, because it lies under the whole weight of the ocean, is uncovered by God's breath as easily as dust is blown from a table. Isaiah uses the same word for a flood of a different sort: Assyria is a river rising over its banks, “he shall come up over all his channels, and go over all his banks” (Isa 8:7), and “he shall pass through Judah; he shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck; and the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel” (Isa 8:8). The invasion rises to the neck and no further, and the chapter halts it with a name — Immanuel, God with us.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a channel as the hollow bed of a river or stream of water; a canal; the deeper part of a strait, bay or harbor.
webster_full: CHAN'NEL, n. In a general sense, a passage; a place of passing or flowing; particularly, the place where a river flows, including the whole breadth of the river.
2. The deeper part of a strait, bay or harbor, where the main current flows.
3. That through which any thing passes; means of passing, conveying or transmitting.
BANK, n. The margin of a watercourse; the rising ground bordering a river.
scriptures: Psalm 18:15
Then the channels of waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were discovered at thy rebuke, O LORD, at the blast of the breath of thy nostrils.
2 Samuel 22:16
And the channels of the sea appeared, the foundations of the world were discovered, at the rebuking of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.
Isaiah 8:7

Now therefore, behold, the Lord bringeth up upon them the waters of the river, strong and many, even the king of Assyria, and all his glory: and he shall come up over all his channels, and go over all his banks:
Isaiah 8:8
And he shall pass through Judah; he shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck; and the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel.
corruption_summary: Empires and disasters are read as forces in their own right, when Isaiah says plainly that the Lord brings up the river and fixes how far it rises.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 8:7 does not say Assyria rose against Judah; it says the Lord bringeth up upon them the waters of the river, even the king of Assyria. The empire is the instrument; the hand is God's. This is the harder half of providence and the church has always found ways round it — God permitted, God allowed, God did not prevent. Scripture uses the active voice. And the same sentence that gives the flood its author gives it its limit: it reaches to the neck. A river that God brings does not drown the people God keeps, and the chapter names the reason in a single word, Immanuel.

The psalms of deliverance make the same point from the other direction. When God rebukes, the channels of the sea appear and the foundations of the world are uncovered — that is, what is deepest, most hidden, and most permanent in creation is laid open by His breath. Every account of the world in which its underlying structures are simply there, immovable and unaddressed, is answered by this image. The believer's comfort is not that the waters are shallow but that the One who made the channels is the One who commands them.
roots_summary: Hebrew aphiq (H650), a channel, watercourse, or strong containing bed — 2 Samuel 22:16, Psalm 18:15, Isaiah 8:7, Psalm 42:1 of the water brooks.
roots_lines: Hebrew aphiq (H650) — a channel or watercourse; 2 Samuel 22:16, Psalm 18:15, Psalm 42:1, Ezekiel 6:3.
Hebrew mosad (H4146) — foundation; the companion word, the foundations of the world uncovered.
Hebrew gaarah (H1606) — a rebuke; what dries the channels, as at the Red Sea.
Hebrew ruach appo — the breath of his nostrils; the same phrase used in Exodus 15:8 of the sea standing upright.
Isaiah 8:8 fixes the flood's limit at the neck, and names the reason: O Immanuel.
usage: “The channels of the sea appeared… at the blast of the breath of his nostrils”.
“The Lord bringeth up upon them the waters of the river” — the active voice.
“He shall reach even to the neck” — and no further, O Immanuel.

pos: n. pl. (standing waters of Egypt, struck in the plagues — Hebrew agam)
etymology: From pound, an enclosure, hence a body of water shut in. The Hebrew agam is a marshy pool or standing water, distinguished from a running stream.
biblical_def: The ponds of Egypt appear in the plagues, in the LORD's own inventory of every water in the land. “Say unto Aaron, Take thy rod, and stretch out thine hand upon the waters of Egypt, upon their streams, upon their rivers, and upon their ponds, and upon all their pools of water, that they may become blood; and that there may be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood, and in vessels of stone” (Exo 7:19). Nothing is left out: streams, rivers, ponds, pools, and even the water already drawn and standing in a wooden bucket or a stone jar. The judgment is total by design, because the Nile was worshipped and the LORD said He would execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. The frogs come out of the same waters: “Stretch forth thine hand with thy rod over the streams, over the rivers, and over the ponds, and cause frogs to come up upon the land of Egypt” (Exo 8:5). Isaiah later foretells the day when Egypt's water economy fails altogether: “the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up” (Isa 19:5), and “they shall be broken in the purposes thereof, all that make sluices and ponds for fish” (Isa 19:10). A nation built on a river is broken by the God who made the river.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pond as a body of stagnant water without an outlet, larger than a puddle, and smaller than a lake; or a collection of water in a reservoir.
webster_full: POND, n. A body of stagnant water without an outlet, larger than a puddle, and smaller than a lake; or a like body of water with a small outlet.
2. A collection of water raised in a river by a dam, for the purpose of propelling mill wheels.
POOL, n. A small collection of water in a hollow place, supplied by a spring, and discharging its surplus water by an outlet.
SLUICE, n. A frame of timber, stone or metal, serving to stop and confine water, or to let it pass.
scriptures: Exodus 7:19

And the LORD spake unto Moses, Say unto Aaron, Take thy rod, and stretch out thine hand upon the waters of Egypt, upon their streams, upon their rivers, and upon their ponds, and upon all their pools of water, that they may become blood; and that there may be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood, and in vessels of stone.
Exodus 8:5
And the LORD spake unto Moses, Say unto Aaron, Stretch forth thine hand with thy rod over the streams, over the rivers, and over the ponds, and cause frogs to come up upon the land of Egypt.
Isaiah 19:10
And they shall be broken in the purposes thereof, all that make sluices and ponds for fish.
Isaiah 19:5
And the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up.
corruption_summary: The plagues are explained away as natural phenomena in sequence, and the point Exodus states — judgment upon the gods of Egypt — is dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: A long tradition of commentary explains the plagues as a chain of natural events: red silt in the Nile, frogs fleeing the fouled water, flies breeding on the dead frogs. Some such means may well have been used, since God ordinarily works through what He has made. But the explanation is not a substitute for the text, which reports the timing announced beforehand, the exemption of Goshen, the beginning and ending at Moses' word, and the LORD's own stated purpose — against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment. A natural sequence that begins when a man lifts a rod and stops when he prays is not an alternative to a miracle; it is one.

The care of the inventory in Exodus 7:19 makes the same point in miniature. Streams, rivers, ponds, pools, and the water in wooden and stone vessels — the judgment reaches the water already in the house, the water a household had carried and stored against exactly such trouble. The Nile was the life and the god of Egypt, and the first plague turned the god into a stench. Isaiah 19 finishes the argument centuries later: the men who make sluices and ponds for fish shall be broken in their purposes, because a civilization is only as secure as the God who governs its river.

Hebrew yeor (H2975) — the Nile, the river of Egypt; the deity of the land and the first thing struck.

The inventory reaches the water in vessels of wood and stone — what was already drawn and stored.

pos: n. (marsh-grass by the Nile where the kine fed — Hebrew achu)
etymology: Old English mædwe, mowing land. The Hebrew achu is a word of Egyptian origin for the reed-grass of the Nile bank — the pasture that only the river makes.
biblical_def: Meadow occurs in the Authorized Version in one place: Pharaoh's dream. “And, behold, there came up out of the river seven well favoured kine and fatfleshed; and they fed in a meadow” (Gen 41:2), and Pharaoh repeats it in his own telling: “there came up out of the river seven kine, fatfleshed and well favoured; and they fed in a meadow” (Gen 41:18). The Hebrew word is Egyptian, the reed-grass of the Nile bank, and the detail is exact: in Egypt fat cattle mean a full river, since the pasture comes up where the flood has been. Then “the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke” (Gen 41:4). The magicians of Egypt could not read it; a Hebrew prisoner could, and refused the credit before he began: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace” (Gen 41:16). Seven years of plenty and seven of famine were coming, the dream was doubled because the thing was established by God, and God would shortly bring it to pass. The meadow is a small word in the account, but it is the hinge of a providence that preserved Jacob's house alive and put a Hebrew over the granaries of the world.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a meadow as a tract of low land, usually appropriated to the culture of grass; and notes that in the Scriptures it renders a word for the reed grass of the Nile.
webster_full: MEAD'OW, n. A tract of low land, appropriated to the production of grass or hay.
2. In the Scriptures, low ground by a river, producing rank grass; as, they fed in a meadow.
KINE, n. plural of cow; used in the older English and retained in the Authorized Version.
FAT'FLESHED, a. Having a plump body; fleshy; well fed.
scriptures: Genesis 41:2
And, behold, there came up out of the river seven well favoured kine and fatfleshed; and they fed in a meadow.
Genesis 41:18
And, behold, there came up out of the river seven kine, fatfleshed and well favoured; and they fed in a meadow:
Genesis 41:4
And the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke.
Genesis 41:16
And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace.
corruption_summary: Providence is reduced to coincidence, and the interpreter's disclaimer — it is not in me — is exactly what modern religious expertise refuses to say.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Joseph's first sentence before Pharaoh. Brought out of a dungeon, shaved and changed, standing before the most powerful man on earth who had just been told that this Hebrew could interpret dreams, Joseph said: It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. Every ministry lives or dies at that sentence. The man who accepts the credit offered him for what God does through him has begun to steal, and the theft is nearly invisible because everything he says afterward may still be true.

The chapter also displays a providence that is complete before it is visible. The meadow grass grew because the river rose; the river rose for seven years and then failed for seven; a dream came to a heathen king; a forgotten butler remembered a prisoner; and a family in Canaan was preserved alive through a famine that would otherwise have ended the line of promise. None of the parties saw the design at the time, and Joseph himself only stated it years later to his frightened brothers: ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good. That is how providence is normally read — backwards, and only by faith.
roots_summary: Hebrew achu (H260), reed-grass, meadow of the Nile bank — Genesis 41:2, 41:18, Job 8:11; a word of Egyptian origin, fitting an Egyptian scene.
roots_lines: Hebrew achu (H260) — reed grass, meadow; Genesis 41:2 and 41:18, and Job 8:11 where the flag grows without water.
Hebrew parah (H6510) — a heifer, cow; the kine of the dream.
The word is of Egyptian derivation, a mark of the narrative's setting rather than a later invention.
In Egypt fat cattle mean a full Nile: the pasture depends entirely on the flood.
Genesis 41:32 explains the doubled dream: the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass.
usage: “They fed in a meadow” — fat cattle mean a full river.
“It is not in me” — the first thing the interpreter said.
The dream was doubled because the thing was established by God.

pos: n. (sap, vital fluid; what a rooted thing draws and a rootless thing lacks — Hebrew lēach, Greek ikmas)
etymology: Latin mustum, new wine, through Old French moiste. The Hebrew lēach means freshness or sap; the Greek ikmas is moisture in the ground.
biblical_def: Moisture in Scripture is sap — the vital fluid that keeps a living thing green — and its absence is used three ways. In the parable of the sower, of the seed on rock: “And some fell upon a rock; and as soon as it was sprung up, it withered away, because it lacked moisture” (Luk 8:6). The Lord Himself interprets it: “They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away” (Luk 8:13). Everything above ground was right — it sprang up quickly, and it was received with joy — and there was nothing beneath. David describes the same drying under conviction of sin: “For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer” (Psa 32:4) — the misery of unconfessed sin in a believer, which he ends in the next verse by acknowledging his transgression. And the word is used once as praise, of Moses at a hundred and twenty: “his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated” (Deu 34:7), where the Hebrew behind natural force is this same word for freshness. Moses died undimmed and unwithered, on the mountain, at the word of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines moisture as a small quantity of any liquid; that which moistens or makes damp; and, of plants, the sap or juice which sustains life.
webster_full: MOIST'URE, n. A small quantity of any liquid; that which moistens or makes damp.
2. In plants, the sap or vital juice; that without which vegetation cannot proceed.
MOIST, a. Moderately wet; damp; not dry.
SAP, n. The juice of plants of any kind, which nourishes and sustains the vegetable.
scriptures: Luke 8:6
And some fell upon a rock; and as soon as it was sprung up, it withered away, because it lacked moisture.
Luke 8:13
They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away.
Psalm 32:4
For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah.
Deuteronomy 34:7
And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated.
corruption_summary: Quick and joyful response to the word is taken for conversion, when the Lord Himself names it as the mark of the rootless ground.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 8:13 is one of the most sobering verses in the Gospels for anyone who measures ministry by response. The rocky ground produced the fastest growth of the four soils, and the reception was joyful; the Lord says of these that they for a while believe, and fall away in time of temptation. What was missing was invisible from the surface: root, and therefore moisture. Where a church counts its harvest by immediate enthusiasm, it will regularly report as fruit what Christ classifies as failure, and it will build methods designed to produce exactly the response He warns about.

The remedy is not to discourage joy. Both the second and the fourth soils receive the word; the difference is depth, and depth is a matter of what happens where no one is watching — in the closet, in the daily reading, in the hard obedience nobody applauds. David's dried-up moisture in Psalm 32 shows what it feels like when a real believer stops drinking: heaviness, wasting, the drought of summer, until he says I acknowledged my sin unto thee and the drought breaks. And Deuteronomy 34 shows the other end — a man of a hundred and twenty, undimmed and unwithered, because for forty years he had been drinking of that spiritual Rock that followed them.

Hebrew lēach (H3893) — freshness, moisture, natural force; Deuteronomy 34:7, Jeremiah 11:16 of the green olive tree.
Hebrew lěshad (H3955) — sap or vital moisture; Psalm 32:4, Numbers 11:8 of the taste of the manna.
Greek rhiza (G4491) — root; what the rocky ground lacked, and the reason the moisture failed.
Psalm 1:3 and Jeremiah 17:8 give the opposite case: a tree planted by the waters whose leaf shall be green.

“Which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away”.
“Nor his natural force abated” — Moses undimmed at a hundred and twenty.

pos: n. and v. (a place one frequents; to resort to habitually — Hebrew regel, the foot)
etymology: Old French hanter, to frequent. The Hebrew idiom in 1 Samuel 23:22 is literally where his foot shall be — a man's haunt is where his feet keep taking him.
biblical_def: A haunt in the Authorized Version is simply a place a man frequents, with none of the ghostly sense the word later acquired. Saul, hunting David, gives the order: “Go, I pray you, prepare yet, and know and see his place where his haunt is, and who hath seen him there: for it is told me that he dealeth very subtilly” (1Sa 23:22) — and the Hebrew margin reads, literally, where his foot shall be. After Ziklag, David sends spoil “to them which were in Hebron, and to all the places where David himself and his men were wont to haunt” (1Sa 30:31); the outlaw remembered every town that had sheltered him, and paid it back. Ezekiel uses the verb of Tyre: the renowned city “which cause their terror to be on all that haunt it” (Eze 26:17). The word therefore describes something worth examining in any life: the places a man's feet habitually take him. Saul thought that knowing David's haunts would deliver him; the Psalmist knew there is no haunt outside God's sight, and made it a comfort rather than a threat: “Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?” (Psa 139:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines haunt as to frequent; to resort to much or often; and as a noun, a place of frequent resort; a customary place of meeting.
webster_full: HAUNT, v.t. To frequent; to resort to much or often, or to be much about; to visit customarily.
2. To come to frequently; to appear often; as, a spirit is said to haunt a place.
HAUNT, n. A place to which one frequently resorts; a customary place of resort.
RESORT', v.i. To have recourse; to go; to repair; to frequent.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 23:22
Go, I pray you, prepare yet, and know and see his place where his haunt is, and who hath seen him there: for it is told me that he dealeth very subtilly.
1 Samuel 30:31
And to them which were in Hebron, and to all the places where David himself and his men were wont to haunt.
Ezekiel 26:17

And they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and say to thee, How art thou destroyed, that wast inhabited of seafaring men, the renowned city, which wast strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, which cause their terror to be on all that haunt it!
Psalm 139:7
Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
corruption_summary: The word has been captured by the occult and lost to its plain use, and with it the plain question of where a man's feet habitually take him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Saul was after for the wrong reason: a man is known by his haunts. Where the feet go by habit, the heart has already gone, and no profession of faith survives a settled contradiction between the two. The Hebrew idiom is worth keeping in mind because it removes all abstraction — where his foot shall be. A man may be uncertain about many things in his own heart; he is rarely uncertain about where he spends his evenings.

David's use of the word in 1 Samuel 30 is the finest thing in the entry. He had been a fugitive; certain towns had fed him and hidden him and asked nothing; and when he came into spoil he sent portions to every one of them by name. Gratitude with a long memory and an open hand is one of the marks of a converted man. And Psalm 139 turns the whole subject God-ward: there is no haunt out of His sight, which terrifies the man running from Him and steadies the man running to Him — the same omniscience, read two ways.

Hebrew maqom (H4725) — a place, standing spot; the plain word for the location Saul sought.

Psalm 139:7 sets every haunt under God's eye, which is threat or comfort depending on which way a man is running.
usage: “Know and see his place where his haunt is” — literally, where his foot shall be.
“All the places where David himself and his men were wont to haunt” — and he paid every one back.
“Whither shall I flee from thy presence?” — there is no haunt outside His sight.

pos: v. and adj. (lying hid to ambush — Hebrew machaboim, hiding places)
etymology: Middle English lurken, to lie hid, of Scandinavian origin. The word always carries intent: not merely concealed, but concealed in order to strike.
biblical_def: Lurking in Scripture is concealment with intent. Saul commands a search: “See therefore, and take knowledge of all the lurking places where he hideth himself, and come ye again to me with the certainty” (1Sa 23:23) — the pursuit of an innocent man described in the language of hunting vermin. The Psalmist uses it of the wicked, and the picture is a predator: “He sitteth in the lurking places of the villages: in the secret places doth he murder the innocent: his eyes are privily set against the poor” (Psa 10:8), and “Like as a lion that is greedy of his prey, and as it were a young lion lurking in secret places” (Psa 17:12). Note where the lurking happens: in the villages, not in the wilderness. The predator of Psalm 10 lives among his victims and is known to them, and his eyes are privily set against the poor because the poor cannot answer him. The next verse completes the hunt: “He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to catch the poor: he doth catch the poor, when he draweth him into his net” (Psa 10:9). Three times in two verses, the poor. Scripture does not describe predation in the abstract; it names the class that is preyed upon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lurking as lying hid; lying in wait; keeping out of sight, especially for the purpose of ambush or evil design.
webster_full: LURK'ING, ppr. Lying concealed; keeping out of sight.
LURK, v.i. To lie hid; to lie in wait; to lie concealed or unperceived.
2. To keep out of sight, with a purpose of doing evil.
AMBUSH, n. A private or concealed station, where troops lie in wait to attack an enemy by surprise.
scriptures: Psalm 10:8
He sitteth in the lurking places of the villages: in the secret places doth he murder the innocent: his eyes are privily set against the poor.
Psalm 10:9
He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to catch the poor: he doth catch the poor, when he draweth him into his net.
1 Samuel 23:23

See therefore, and take knowledge of all the lurking places where he hideth himself, and come ye again to me with the certainty, and I will go with you: and it shall come to pass, if he be in the land, that I will search him out throughout all the thousands of Judah.
Psalm 17:12
Like as a lion that is greedy of his prey, and as it were a young lion lurking in secret places.
corruption_summary: Predation upon the weak is treated as a private failing when it is discovered, rather than as the settled practice Psalm 10 says it is.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 10 is not describing an outburst but a business. The man sits in the lurking places of the villages; his eyes are privily set; he lieth in wait as a lion in his den; he draws the poor into his net. Every verb is habitual and every one is planned. When such conduct comes to light, the standard defence is that it was uncharacteristic — a lapse, a moment. Scripture's account is that the lurking came first and the seizure followed, and that the seizure will happen again as soon as the cover is restored. This is why the Psalm ends by asking God to break the arm of the wicked and to seek out his wickedness till He find none.

The Psalm also fixes attention on who is taken. Three times in one verse: the poor. Predators choose targets who cannot answer, cannot afford a lawyer, will not be believed, or have nowhere else to go — and the choosing is deliberate, which is why God's repeated self-description as the helper of the fatherless is not sentiment but jurisdiction. A church that protects its reputation by quieting such a case has placed itself on the wrong side of Psalm 10, and the same Psalm says the LORD is King for ever and ever, and will hear the desire of the humble.
roots_summary: Hebrew machaboim (H4224), hiding places — 1 Samuel 23:23; arab (H693), to lie in wait, ambush — Psalm 10:9; mistar (H4565), a secret place — Psalm 10:8, 17:12.

Hebrew mistar (H4565) — a secret or covert place; Psalm 10:8, Psalm 17:12, Habakkuk 3:14.
Hebrew cheleka (H2489) — the poor, the hapless; the repeated object in Psalm 10.

“His eyes are privily set against the poor” — the target is chosen.
“He lieth in wait to catch the poor” — a settled business, not an outburst.

pos: n. pl. (inhabitants; those who dwell in a place — Greek katoikountes)
etymology: From dwell, Old English dwellan, originally to lead astray or tarry, later to reside. The Greek katoikeo means to settle down and live in a place, as distinct from sojourning.
biblical_def: Dwellers are the settled inhabitants of a place, and Luke uses the word twice at the birth of the church. Of the field bought with the betrayal money: “And it was known unto all the dwellers at Jerusalem; insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood” (Act 1:19) — the whole city knew, and the name stuck. Then at Pentecost, in the roll-call of nations: “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia” (Act 2:9). These were not tourists; Luke says “there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven” (Act 2:5). Men who had come from the ends of the empire and settled in the city heard the wonderful works of God each in the tongue of the country he had left. The gospel that would go to every nation began by being preached to representatives of every nation who had already come home. Isaiah addresses the same wide audience: “All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth, see ye, when he lifteth up an ensign on the mountains; and when he bloweth a trumpet, hear ye” (Isa 18:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dweller as an inhabitant; a resident of some continuance in a place; one who has a fixed habitation.
webster_full: DWELL'ER, n. An inhabitant; a resident of some continuance in a place.
DWELL, v.i. To abide as a permanent resident, or to inhabit for a time; to live in a place.
2. To be in any state or condition; to continue.
INHAB'ITANT, n. A dweller; one who dwells or resides permanently in a place.
scriptures: Acts 1:19
And it was known unto all the dwellers at Jerusalem; insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood.
Acts 2:9
Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia,
Acts 2:5
And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.
Isaiah 18:3
All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth, see ye, when he lifteth up an ensign on the mountains; and when he bloweth a trumpet, hear ye.
corruption_summary: Pentecost is treated as an ecstatic experience rather than the intelligible preaching of the works of God to settled men from every nation.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke's list of dwellers is the point of the miracle and is regularly passed over in favour of the sound and the fire. What the crowd reported was not confusion but comprehension: we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God. Every man heard intelligible speech about God's acts in the language of the country he came from. Where the day is preached chiefly as an experience to be repeated, the content disappears, and what is sought is the sensation rather than the works of God declared in a language the hearer can understand. Paul later ruled the whole subject in Corinth by exactly this standard: in the church he would rather speak five words with his understanding than ten thousand in an unknown tongue.

The other detail worth holding is the honesty of Acts 1:19. Peter, standing before the assembled believers, tells the plain story of Judas — the field, the money, the name the whole city had given the place, the field of blood. He does not tidy it. A movement inventing its credentials does not open its first chapter with the suicide of one of its founding twelve and a piece of ground the neighbours had already renamed after the scandal. The dwellers at Jerusalem all knew; Luke says so, and writes it down anyway.

pos: n. (a settled habitation; what the apostles did not have — Hebrew moshab, Greek astateo)
etymology: A compound of dwelling and place. The Greek behind 1 Corinthians 4:11 is a single verb, astateo, meaning to be unsettled, to have no fixed standing place.
biblical_def: Dwellingplace is a settled habitation, and Scripture uses it to mark three conditions. Balaam looks at the Kenites and admires their security: “Strong is thy dwellingplace, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock” (Num 24:21) — and the oracle goes on to say that the Kenite shall be wasted nonetheless. Jeremiah announces the end of an empire: “Babylon shall become heaps, a dwellingplace for dragons, an astonishment, and an hissing, without an inhabitant” (Jer 51:37) — the strongest city on earth reduced to a lair for wild creatures. And Paul describes the apostolic ministry: “Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace” (1Co 4:11). The men through whom the New Testament came had no address. Set beside the Corinthians whom Paul is ironically congratulating — full, rich, reigning as kings — the contrast is the whole argument of the chapter. Hebrews states the settled doctrine: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). A nest in a rock is wasted; a city of empires becomes a den; the apostles had nothing; and the church looks for a city whose builder and maker is God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dwelling place as the place of residence; an abode; a habitation; the place where one lives.
webster_full: DWELLING-PLACE, n. The place of residence; abode; habitation.
DWELL'ING, n. Habitation; place of residence; abode.
HABITA'TION, n. Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode; settled dwelling.
CONTIN'UING, ppr. Remaining fixed or permanent; abiding; as, here have we no continuing city.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 4:11
Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace;
Numbers 24:21
And he looked on the Kenites, and took up his parable, and said, Strong is thy dwellingplace, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock.
Jeremiah 51:37
And Babylon shall become heaps, a dwellingplace for dragons, an astonishment, and an hissing, without an inhabitant.
Hebrews 13:14
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
corruption_summary: Comfort and security are treated as the natural marks of God's favour on a ministry, and the apostles' actual conditions are read as an unfortunate early stage the church has since outgrown.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 4 is written against exactly this instinct, and its irony is savage: now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us — and then the apostles' own inventory, hunger, thirst, nakedness, buffeting, no certain dwellingplace. Paul is not commending poverty for its own sake; he is exposing a church that had adopted the world's measures of success and consequently despised the men who had brought them the gospel. Any ministry judged by its comfort will end by judging the apostles deficient, which is precisely the position Paul mocks.

Hebrews 13:14 gives the doctrine that keeps this from becoming mere asceticism. Here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come. The Christian is not homeless; he is between homes, and the one he seeks is permanent. That is why Balaam's Kenite nest in the rock — genuinely strong, genuinely admired — is still wasted, and why Babylon's vast permanence becomes a dwellingplace for dragons. Every earthly security is provisional, and the man who knows it is free to use one gratefully and lose it without despair.

pos: adj. (outermost; the farthest edge or border — Hebrew qatseh, an extremity)
etymology: From out and the superlative ending -most. The older English form of outermost, retained by the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Outmost means the farthest edge, and Scripture uses it of curtains, of borders, and of the reach of God's gathering hand. Of the tabernacle: “thou shalt make fifty loops on the edge of the one curtain that is outmost in the coupling, and fifty loops in the edge of the curtain which coupleth the second” (Exo 26:10) — the very margin of the sanctuary's fabric was measured and fastened by command. Of the land: “your south border shall be the outmost coast of the salt sea eastward” (Num 34:3), the boundary of the inheritance drawn by God, not negotiated by tribes. And, greatest of all, of the scattered: “If any of thine be driven out unto the outmost parts of heaven, from thence will the LORD thy God gather thee, and from thence will he fetch thee” (Deu 30:4). That promise was made before the exile happened, in the same chapter that foretold it, and Nehemiah pleaded it in Babylon centuries later: “though there were of you cast out unto the uttermost part of the heaven, yet will I gather them from thence, and will bring them unto the place that I have chosen to set my name there” (Neh 1:9). The furthest edge conceivable to the Hebrew mind — the outmost parts of heaven — is named as within reach of the God who gathers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines outmost as furthest from the middle or interior part; utmost; outermost.
webster_full: OUT'MOST, a. Furthest from the middle or interior part; most remote; utmost.
UT'MOST, a. Extreme; being in the greatest or highest degree; furthest.
BOR'DER, n. The outer edge of any thing; the extreme part or surrounding line; the confine or exterior limit of a country.
COAST, n. The exterior line, limit or border of a country; the edge or margin of the land next to the sea.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 30:4
If any of thine be driven out unto the outmost parts of heaven, from thence will the LORD thy God gather thee, and from thence will he fetch thee:
Nehemiah 1:9

But if ye turn unto me, and keep my commandments, and do them; though there were of you cast out unto the uttermost part of the heaven, yet will I gather them from thence, and will bring them unto the place that I have chosen to set my name there.
Exodus 26:10
And thou shalt make fifty loops on the edge of the one curtain that is outmost in the coupling, and fifty loops in the edge of the curtain which coupleth the second.
Numbers 34:3
Then your south quarter shall be from the wilderness of Zin along by the coast of Edom, and your south border shall be the outmost coast of the salt sea eastward:
corruption_summary: Distance is treated as a real obstacle to God — a man too far gone, a people too far scattered — and Deuteronomy 30:4 names the furthest edge imaginable and says God fetches from there.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach stated in Deuteronomy 30:4. The promise was given before the scattering, in the chapter that predicted it, and it names the extreme limit of the ancient imagination — the outmost parts of heaven — only in order to say that God gathers from there and fetches from there. Two verbs, both active, both His. No exile is far enough to be out of range, and no sinner has wandered past the edge of that sentence.

Nehemiah's use shows how such a promise is to be handled. In Susa, hearing that the wall of Jerusalem was broken down, he did not merely grieve; he prayed the promise back to God almost word for word, with its condition attached — if ye turn unto me, and keep my commandments, and do them. That is the pattern of believing prayer: find what God has said, plead it in His hearing, and accept the terms He set with it. And the last clause names the destination as well as the rescue: not merely gathered from the ends of the earth, but brought unto the place He has chosen to set His name there.

roots_lines: Hebrew qatseh (H7097) — an end, extremity; Deuteronomy 30:4, Isaiah 40:28 of the ends of the earth.

“The outmost coast of the salt sea eastward” — a border drawn by God.
