pos: adj. (furthest within; the deepest part — Hebrew cheder, an inner chamber)
etymology: From inner and -most. The Hebrew cheder is an inner room, and the phrase in Proverbs is literally the chambers of the belly — the innermost rooms of a man.
biblical_def: Innermost occurs twice in the Authorized Version, and both times it is the same sentence, repeated word for word in Proverbs: “The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly” (Pro 18:8; Pro 26:22). Solomon says it twice because it needs saying twice. The Hebrew is literally the chambers of the belly — the inner rooms of a man — and the image is of something swallowed like a delicacy and lodged where it cannot be reached. That is what gossip does. It is received with appetite, it goes deep, and it stays. A slander heard about a brother alters how he is seen years after the report is forgotten and long after it has been proved false, because it did not stay on the surface where reason could get at it. The surrounding proverbs give the remedy: “Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth” (Pro 26:20). Strife needs fuel and the talebearer supplies it; remove the supply and the fire dies. James names the same organ and the same fire: “the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity… and it is set on fire of hell” (Jas 3:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines innermost as furthest inward; most remote from the surface or external part; and notes the scriptural phrase, the innermost parts of the belly.
webster_full: IN'NERMOST, a. Furthest inward; most remote from the surface or external part.
IN'NER, a. Interior; further inward than something else; internal.
TALEBEARER, n. A person who officiously tells tales; one who impertinently communicates intelligence or anecdotes, and makes mischief in society.
WOUND, n. A breach of the skin and flesh of an animal, or of the bark and wood of a tree, or of the substance of other bodies.
scriptures: Proverbs 18:8
The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.
Proverbs 26:22
The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.
Proverbs 26:20
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
James 3:6
And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell.
corruption_summary: Gossip is defended as information, prayer request, or accountability, and its permanence in the hearer is not reckoned with at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Solomon's point is not that gossip is unkind — everybody knows that — but that it is permanent. The words go down into the innermost parts, past the place where a man weighs evidence, and they lodge there. This is why a retraction never repairs a slander: the correction is filed in the mind, the original is filed in the chambers of the belly, and the two are not in the same room. Anyone who has heard a false report about a brother and found, years later, that his instinctive reaction to that man is still coloured by it, has felt the proverb work.

The excuses under which the traffic runs in churches are worth naming: sharing so that others can pray, providing context, being transparent, holding people accountable. Some of these are genuine duties, and Scripture provides for them — go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone, and the two or three witnesses, and the church. What every one of those procedures has in common is that the person spoken about is present or is going to be. The talebearer's distinctive is that his subject is not in the room and will never be told. Proverbs 26:20 gives the practical rule, and it is aimed at the hearer as much as the speaker: no wood, no fire.
roots_summary: Hebrew cheder (H2315), an inner chamber — in the phrase chambers of the belly, Proverbs 18:8, 26:22, 20:27; nirgan (H5372), a talebearer or whisperer.
roots_lines: Hebrew cheder (H2315) — an inner room or chamber; Proverbs 18:8 and 26:22, and Proverbs 20:27 of the inward parts searched by the LORD's candle.
Hebrew nirgan (H5372) — a whisperer, talebearer; Proverbs 16:28, 18:8, 26:20, 26:22.
Hebrew beten (H990) — the belly, the seat of what is taken in and kept.
Greek psithuristes (G5588) — a whisperer; Romans 1:29, the New Testament counterpart.
The verse is repeated verbatim in two chapters of Proverbs, which is itself the emphasis.
usage: “They go down into the innermost parts of the belly” — and they stay.
“Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out” — a rule for the hearer too.
A retraction never reaches the room the slander went into.

pos: adj. (highest in place or rank; the chief seat — Greek protoklisia, the first couch)
etymology: From upper and -most. In the Gospels the phrase uppermost rooms renders protoklisia, the first place at table, where the couches were ranked by honour.
biblical_def: Uppermost is the highest place, and the Lord Jesus uses it in His indictment of the scribes and Pharisees: they “love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues” (Mat 23:6). The word rendered rooms means the first couch at the table; at an ancient feast the places were ranked, everybody knew the ranking, and the seating was a public statement about a man's standing. The Lord does not object to the existence of order; He objects to the loving of it — a religion whose satisfactions are positional. His own instruction reverses the movement: “when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher” (Luk 14:10). The word appears elsewhere in plain description: the chief baker's dream, “in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head” (Gen 40:17); and Isaiah's picture of desolation, “his strong cities be as a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation” (Isa 17:9). The highest branch is the one the gleaners could not reach and the harvesters abandoned — height and emptiness together.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines uppermost as highest in place; highest in power or authority; predominant.
webster_full: UP'PERMOST, a. Highest in place; as the uppermost seats.
2. Highest in power or authority; predominant; as, ambition was uppermost in his mind.
UP'PER, a. Higher; superior in place; as the upper story.
ROOM, n. Place; space; in the Scriptures, a place at table, as the uppermost rooms at feasts.
scriptures: Matthew 23:6
And love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues,
Luke 14:10

But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee.
Isaiah 17:9
In that day shall his strong cities be as a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation.
Genesis 40:17
And in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head.
corruption_summary: Position within the church is sought and defended as though it were the point of ministry, and the Lord's reversal is admired without being obeyed.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 23:6 names an appetite, not an office: they love the uppermost rooms. The scribes had real authority and sat in Moses' seat, and the Lord told the people to observe what they said. The sin was the loving — the enjoyment of the position for its own sake, the greetings in the markets, the title. Every generation of the church reproduces it with its own currencies: the platform, the byline, the reputation among peers, the seat at the right table. It is not detected by asking whether a man holds a high place but whether he loves it, and the test appears the moment the place is threatened.

Luke 14:10 is regularly misread as a technique. Sit low and be called higher — a strategy for gaining honour by declining it, which would leave the appetite entirely intact and merely change its method. The Lord closes that reading in the next verse: whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted. The exalting is God's act and is not extracted by arrangement. And the parable that follows tells the host to invite those who cannot recompense him — the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind — which is the same doctrine applied where no seating chart can flatter anybody.
roots_summary: Greek protoklisia (G4411), the chief reclining place at a feast — Matthew 23:6, Luke 14:7, Mark 12:39; protokathedria (G4410), the chief seat in the synagogue; Hebrew elyon (H5945), upper, highest.
roots_lines: Greek protoklisia (G4411) — the first couch, chief place at table; Matthew 23:6, Mark 12:39, Luke 14:7-8, Luke 20:46.
Greek protokathedria (G4410) — the chief seat; the companion phrase, of the synagogues.
Hebrew elyon (H5945) — upper, uppermost, and also the divine title Most High.
Hebrew amir (H534) — a topmost bough; Isaiah 17:6 and 17:9.
Luke 14:11 supplies the rule the whole passage rests on: he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
usage: “Love the uppermost rooms at feasts” — the sin is in the loving.
“Go and sit down in the lowest room” — and it is not a technique.
“A forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch” — height and emptiness together.

pos: adv. (head foremost; with violent precipitation — Greek prenes and katakremnizo)
etymology: From head and the old adverbial ending -ling. It means head first, and by extension rashly, without stopping to consider.
biblical_def: Headlong in Scripture describes a fall that cannot be arrested. Of Judas: “Now this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out” (Act 1:18). Peter reports the end of a man who had walked three years with the Lord, and does not soften it. Of the crowd at Nazareth, who had just heard the sweetest sermon ever preached in their synagogue: they “rose up, and thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong” (Luk 4:29). The neighbours who had watched Him grow up tried to throw Him off a cliff, and the reason was His saying that God's mercy had gone to a Sidonian widow and a Syrian leper. “But he passing through the midst of them went his way” (Luk 4:30) — His hour was not yet come, and no hill could take Him before it. Job supplies the proverb underneath both scenes: “He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong” (Job 5:13). Schemes laid against God gather their own momentum and go over the edge with the schemer aboard.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines headlong as with the head foremost; rashly; precipitately; without deliberation; hastily.
webster_full: HEAD'LONG, adv. With the head foremost; as, to fall headlong.
2. Rashly; precipitately; without deliberation.
3. Hastily; without delay or respite.
PRECIP'ITATE, v.t. To throw headlong; to urge or press on with eagerness or violence.
scriptures: Acts 1:18
Now this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.
Luke 4:29
And rose up, and thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong.
Luke 4:30
But he passing through the midst of them went his way,
Job 5:13
He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong.
corruption_summary: Judas is refashioned as a misunderstood idealist or a necessary instrument, and Nazareth's murderous rage at a sermon is passed over as a local quarrel.
corruption_paragraphs: A long line of writers has tried to rescue Judas — a patriot forcing the Lord's hand, a man playing an assigned part, even a truer disciple than the rest. Scripture leaves no opening. He was a thief who carried the bag, he sold his Master for thirty pieces, the Lord called him the son of perdition, and Peter says he went to his own place. The field was purchased with the reward of iniquity and he fell headlong in it. That God used the betrayal to accomplish redemption does not convert the traitor into an instrument innocent of his act; Acts 2:23 holds both truths in one sentence, the determinate counsel of God and the wicked hands.

Luke 4 is equally unwelcome and equally plain. The congregation at Nazareth began by wondering at the gracious words which proceeded out of His mouth, and ended, within minutes, trying to throw Him off a cliff. What turned them was not a claim of deity but two examples from their own Scriptures in which God's mercy went to Gentiles — a widow of Sarepta and Naaman the Syrian. The offence was grace given outside the expected boundary. Any congregation that hears that doctrine calmly should ask whether it has understood it, and any preacher whose hearers are never once offended should ask what he is preaching.
roots_summary: Greek prenes (G4248), headlong, prone — Acts 1:18 only; katakremnizo (G2630), to throw down a precipice — Luke 4:29 only; Hebrew mahar (H4116), to hasten, in Job 5:13.
roots_lines: Greek prenes (G4248) — headlong, falling forward; Acts 1:18, its only occurrence.
Greek katakremnizo (G2630) — to cast down headlong from a cliff; Luke 4:29, its only occurrence.
Hebrew mahar (H4116) — to hasten, be carried headlong; Job 5:13.
Job 5:13 is quoted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:19 — He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
Luke 4:30 records the plain fact that ends the scene: He passed through the midst of them and went His way.
usage: “Falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst” — Peter does not soften it.
“That they might cast him down headlong” — the response to a sermon on grace to Gentiles.
“The counsel of the froward is carried headlong” — schemes gather their own momentum.

pos: v. and n. (to part in two; in the phrase in sunder, apart — Hebrew qatsats and gada)
etymology: Old English sundrian, to separate, from sundor, apart. The Authorized Version uses it almost always in the phrase in sunder — cut, broken, or burst apart.
biblical_def: Sunder means to part in two, and in the Authorized Version it is chiefly God who does the sundering, and what He sunders are weapons and chains. Of weapons: “He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire” (Psa 46:9). Of chains: “He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder” (Psa 107:14), and “For he hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder” (Psa 107:16). And of altars: “By this therefore shall the iniquity of Jacob be purged; and this is all the fruit to take away his sin; when he maketh all the stones of the altar as chalkstones that are beaten in sunder, the groves and images shall not stand up” (Isa 27:9). Four objects, one hand. The bow, the spear and the chariot are the instruments of war; the bands, the brazen gates and the iron bars are the furniture of captivity; the altar stones are the apparatus of idolatry. God's sundering is always destructive and always liberating, and Isaiah names the purpose plainly: the breaking of the false altar is how the iniquity of Jacob is purged. What God breaks in His people, He breaks to free them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sunder as to part; to separate; to divide; to disunite in almost any manner; and asunder or in sunder, into parts.
webster_full: SUN'DER, v.t. To part; to separate; to divide; to disunite in almost any manner, either by rending, cutting or breaking.
SUN'DER, n. In sunder, in two; apart; as, to cut a thing in sunder.
ASUN'DER, adv. Apart; into parts; separately; in a divided state.
SUN'DRY, a. Several; divers; more than one or two; from the same root, meaning apart or separate.
scriptures: Psalm 46:9
He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.
Psalm 107:14
He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder.
Psalm 107:16
For he hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder.
Isaiah 27:9

By this therefore shall the iniquity of Jacob be purged; and this is all the fruit to take away his sin; when he maketh all the stones of the altar as chalkstones that are beaten in sunder, the groves and images shall not stand up.
corruption_summary: God's breaking is read only as loss, and the believer resists the sundering of the very things that hold him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the four passages have in common: everything God cuts in sunder is a weapon, a chain, a gate, or an idol's altar. He is not breaking what His people need. The bow and spear He snaps are the instruments by which men destroy each other; the brazen gates and iron bars He shatters are what held them in the dark; the altar stones He beats to chalk are the machinery of the sin that ruined them. A believer under a hard providence, watching something break, may ask which of these four it was, and will more often than not be able to tell.

Psalm 107 puts the sundering in a definite order that repays attention: they sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron, because they rebelled against the words of God — then they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them out of their distresses, and brought them out and brake their bands in sunder. Rebellion, chains, crying, deliverance. The Psalm repeats that cycle four times with four different kinds of men, and ends by saying that whoso is wise will observe these things. The bands do not fall off by themselves, and they do not fall off before the crying.
roots_summary: Hebrew qatsats (H7112), to cut off or in pieces — Psalm 46:9, 107:16; gada (H1438), to hew down or cut asunder; naphats (H5310), to dash in pieces, in Isaiah 27:9.
roots_lines: Hebrew qatsats (H7112) — to cut off, cut in pieces; Psalm 46:9, Psalm 107:16.
Hebrew gada (H1438) — to hew down, cut asunder; used of groves, altars and horns of the wicked.
Hebrew naphats (H5310) — to dash or beat in pieces; Isaiah 27:9 of the altar stones as chalkstones.
Hebrew nathaq (H5423) — to pull apart, break bands; Psalm 107:14, Psalm 2:3 where the kings say let us break their bands.
Psalm 2:3 is the counterfeit: men trying to break God's bands, which is the one sundering that never succeeds.
usage: “He breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder”.
“Brake their bands in sunder” — after they cried unto the LORD.
“The stones of the altar as chalkstones that are beaten in sunder”.

pos: v. (put a vessel out from shore; set sail — Greek anago, to put out to sea)
etymology: Old French lancier, to throw or hurl, from Latin lancea, a lance. To launch is to thrust a vessel out from the land.
biblical_def: Launched is the Authorized Version's word for putting out from shore, and it marks the beginning of several decisive passages. On the lake: “he went into a ship with his disciples: and he said unto them, Let us go over unto the other side of the lake. And they launched forth” (Luk 8:22) — and the storm that followed was the occasion of His rebuking the wind and the raging of the water. At Peter's call: “when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught” (Luk 5:4) — a carpenter telling a fisherman where the fish were, after a night of nothing, and Peter's answer was nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net. In Acts the word carries Paul toward Rome: “entering into a ship of Adramyttium, we launched, meaning to sail by the coasts of Asia” (Act 27:2), and “when we had launched from thence, we sailed under Cyprus, because the winds were contrary” (Act 27:4). Every one of these launchings ran into weather. The Lord slept through one, stilled it, and asked where their faith was; Peter's obedient launch filled two ships to sinking; Paul's voyage ended in shipwreck on Melita with every soul saved, exactly as the angel had told him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines launch as to move or cause to slide from the land into the water; to put out to sea; to begin a new course or enterprise.
webster_full: LAUNCH, v.t. To throw, as a lance; to move or cause to slide from the land into the water; as, to launch a ship.
2. To put out; to send on a course; as, to launch into the deep.
LAUNCH, v.i. To glide, as a ship into the water; to put out to sea; to enter on a new field of activity.
DEEP, n. The sea; the abyss of waters; the ocean.
scriptures: Luke 8:22
Now it came to pass on a certain day, that he went into a ship with his disciples: and he said unto them, Let us go over unto the other side of the lake. And they launched forth.
Luke 5:4
Now when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught.
Acts 27:2
And entering into a ship of Adramyttium, we launched, meaning to sail by the coasts of Asia; one Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us.
Acts 27:4
And when we had launched from thence, we sailed under Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
corruption_summary: Obedience is expected to produce calm passage, and a storm on the way is read as evidence that the launch was a mistake.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 8 is decisive on this point and is regularly ignored. It was the Lord who said let us go over unto the other side, and the boat that went at His word ran into a storm that frightened professional fishermen. Obedience did not prevent the weather; it appointed the meeting. The disciples' error was not in launching but in concluding, when the water came in, that He did not care — carest thou not that we perish? — and His question afterwards was not why they were afraid of the sea but where is your faith? A believer in trouble on a course God gave him is exactly where he ought to be.

Peter's launch adds the other half. He had toiled all night and taken nothing, and he was being told where to fish by a carpenter, in the middle of the day, in deep water, in front of a crowd. His reply is the model of obedient faith: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net. He did not say he expected fish; he said he would do it because of who was speaking. The nets broke and the ships began to sink, and Peter's response was to fall down and say, depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. That is the usual order — obedience first, evidence second, and self-knowledge last of all.
roots_summary: Greek anago (G321), to lead up, put out to sea — Luke 8:22, Acts 27:2, 27:4; epanago (G1877), to put out further — Luke 5:3-4; bathos (G899), the deep.
roots_lines: Greek anago (G321) — to put out to sea, set sail; Luke 8:22, Acts 13:13, Acts 27:2 and 27:4.
Greek epanago (G1877) — to put out further from shore; Luke 5:3 of thrusting out a little, 5:4 of launching into the deep.
Greek bathos (G899) — depth, the deep; Luke 5:4, and Romans 11:33 of the depth of the riches of God.
Greek chalao (G5465) — to let down; the nets in Luke 5:4-5.
Every launching in these passages met weather, and none of them was a mistake.
usage: “Let us go over unto the other side… and they launched forth” — straight into the storm.
“Launch out into the deep” — a carpenter to a fisherman, at the wrong hour.
“The winds were contrary” — and the voyage was still God's.

pos: adj. (violently stormy — Hebrew saar, to storm; Greek tuphonikos)
etymology: Latin tempestas, a storm or season. The Greek tuphonikos in Acts 27:14 gives the English typhoon — a whirlwind.
biblical_def: Tempestuous describes a storm that is more than weather. In Jonah, the sea rises against a fleeing prophet and the sailors know it: “Then said they unto him, What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous” (Jon 1:11), and “the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them” (Jon 1:13). Two things are recorded there that shame much religion: heathen sailors rowed hard to save the man who had brought the storm on them, and only threw him over when they could do nothing else, praying first that innocent blood not be laid to their charge. In Acts the word names the wind that wrecked Paul's ship: “not long after there arose against it a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon” (Act 27:14) — a nor'easter off Crete, and Luke gives it by its sailors' name. And the Psalmist uses the same word of God Himself coming to judge: “Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him” (Psa 50:3). The storm that hunts a runaway prophet, the storm that carries an apostle to Rome by way of shipwreck, and the storm around the throne are all the same word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tempestuous as very stormy; turbulent; agitated by furious winds; and figuratively, violent and boisterous.
webster_full: TEMPEST'UOUS, a. Very stormy; turbulent; agitated by furious winds; boisterous.
TEM'PEST, n. An extensive current of wind, rushing with great velocity and violence; a storm of extreme violence.
2. Any tumult, commotion or violent agitation.
EUROC'LYDON, n. A tempestuous wind of the Levant, blowing from the northeast.
scriptures: Jonah 1:11
Then said they unto him, What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous.
Jonah 1:13
Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them.
Acts 27:14
But not long after there arose against it a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon.
Psalm 50:3
Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him.
corruption_summary: Storms are treated as impersonal systems, so that the plain claim of Jonah 1 — that this sea rose because of one man's disobedience — is dismissed as primitive.
corruption_paragraphs: Jonah 1 makes a claim the modern mind refuses in advance: the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea, and the sea rose because of one man's flight. The sailors, who were not Israelites, cast lots and the lot fell on Jonah, and Jonah agreed with the verdict. Nothing in the chapter treats the storm as coincidence. This does not license the reverse inference — that every calamity may be traced to a particular sin, which the book of Job exists to forbid, and which the Lord denied outright concerning the men on whom the tower of Siloam fell. But it forbids the blanket denial too. God governs weather, and He has more than once used it on a man He intended to keep.

The sailors deserve their own paragraph, because they behave better than the prophet. Told that throwing him overboard would still the sea, they rowed hard for land instead, and only when they could not, prayed: let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not upon us innocent blood. Heathen men, striving to save the servant of God who had endangered them; and the prophet asleep in the hold while they cried each to his god. Jonah's later fury over a withered gourd is of a piece with this: the book is about a man who had the truth and less mercy than the sailors and the Ninevites he despised.
roots_summary: Hebrew saar (H5590), to storm, be tempestuous — Jonah 1:11, 1:13, Psalm 50:3; Greek tuphonikos (G5189), like a whirlwind — Acts 27:14 only.
roots_lines: Hebrew saar (H5590) — to storm, rage, be tempestuous; Jonah 1:11 and 1:13, Psalm 50:3.
Hebrew saarah (H5591) — a whirlwind or tempest; 2 Kings 2:11 of Elijah's ascent, Job 38:1 of the LORD answering out of the whirlwind.
Greek tuphonikos (G5189) — typhoon-like, whirling; Acts 27:14, its only occurrence.
Greek Eurokludon (G2148) — Euroclydon, the northeaster; the sailors' own name for the wind, recorded by Luke.
Jonah 1:4 states the cause plainly: the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea.
usage: “The sea wrought, and was tempestuous” — and the sailors knew why.
“The men rowed hard to bring it to the land” — heathen mercy shaming a prophet.
“It shall be very tempestuous round about him” — the storm around the throne.

pos: n. (the state of the sky; in the Gospels, the sign men can read and the sign they will not — Greek eudia and cheimon)
etymology: Old English weder, air, sky, storm. The Greek eudia is fair weather, literally good sky; cheimon is winter or foul weather.
biblical_def: Weather occurs in the Authorized Version chiefly in the Lord's rebuke to men who could forecast a sky and not a Saviour. “When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red” (Mat 16:2), “And in the morning, It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring. O ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?” (Mat 16:3). The Pharisees and Sadducees had come asking for a sign from heaven — while standing in front of the Man whose works they had already seen. The rebuke is not against reading the weather, which is ordinary wisdom, but against a capacity for evidence that stops exactly where repentance would begin. Job places fair weather under God's hand and joins it to something greater: “Fair weather cometh out of the north: with God is terrible majesty” (Job 37:22). And Solomon uses weather for a lesson in pastoral tact: “As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart” (Pro 25:20) — cheerfulness applied to grief does not warm the mourner; it strips him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines weather as the state of the air or atmosphere with respect to heat or cold, wetness or dryness, calm or storm, clearness or cloudiness.
webster_full: WEATH'ER, n. The state of the air or atmosphere with respect to heat or cold, wetness or dryness, calm or storm, clearness or cloudiness, or any other meteorological phenomena.
2. Change of the state of the air.
WEATH'ER, v.t. To sustain the trying effect of; to bear up against and overcome; as, to weather a storm.
LOW'RING, ppr. Appearing dark, gloomy or threatening, as the sky.
scriptures: Matthew 16:2
He answered and said unto them, When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red.
Matthew 16:3
And in the morning, It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring. O ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?
Fair weather cometh out of the north: with God is terrible majesty.
Proverbs 25:20
As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart.
corruption_summary: Unbelief presents itself as a want of evidence, when the Lord identifies it as a refusal to read evidence already in hand.
corruption_paragraphs: The men who asked for a sign from heaven were competent observers — they read the evening sky and the morning sky and were usually right. The Lord calls them hypocrites, not fools, because the failure was not intellectual. The same faculties that weighed the red sky refused to weigh the healings, the feedings, the cleansed lepers and the raised dead. This is the standing answer to unbelief that presents itself as evidential caution. A man who applies to the claims of Christ a standard he applies nowhere else in his life is not being careful; he is protecting a conclusion he reached before the evidence arrived.

Proverbs 25:20 belongs in this entry for the sake of the heavy-hearted, and it corrects the church rather than the world. Singing songs to a heavy heart is likened to taking away a man's coat in cold weather — well meant, and it leaves him colder. Cheerfulness pressed on grief does not lift it; it isolates the mourner and teaches him to hide. Scripture's instruction is to weep with them that weep, and Job's comforters were at their best in the seven days they said nothing.

pos: n. (a fleeing; the rout of an army — Hebrew nus, to flee; Greek phuge)
etymology: Old English flyht, from fleon, to flee. In the Authorized Version it almost always means fleeing from an enemy, not flying through the air.
biblical_def: Flight in Scripture is the rout of an army or the escape of a people, and the numbers are always God's doing. In the covenant blessings: “five of you shall chase an hundred, and an hundred of you shall put ten thousand to flight: and your enemies shall fall before you by the sword” (Lev 26:8). The song of Moses states the same arithmetic in reverse, as a judgment: “How should one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, except their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had shut them up?” (Deu 32:30). Israel's defeats are as supernatural as her victories, and both are traced to the same hand. Hebrews puts the phrase into the roll of faith: those who “waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens” (Heb 11:34) — and the same chapter lists, without a break, those who were tortured, sawn asunder and slain with the sword, so that faith is credited with both outcomes. The Lord uses the word of a flight yet to come: “pray ye that your flight be not in the winter, neither on the sabbath day” (Mat 24:20). Even the escape of the saints is a matter for prayer about its circumstances, which is a tender detail: He tells them to flee, and tells them to pray about the weather when they do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines flight as the act of fleeing; hasty departure to escape danger; and, of an army, the act of running away in defeat.
webster_full: FLIGHT, n. The act of fleeing; hasty departure; the act of running away, to escape danger or expected evil.
2. The act of flying; a passing through the air by the help of wings.
3. A number of beings or things passing through the air together; as a flight of arrows.
ROUT, n. The defeat and confusion of an army or band of troops; a disorderly flight.

corruption_summary: Victory is claimed as a promise to every believer in every circumstance, and Hebrews 11 lists in one breath those who escaped the sword and those who were slain with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 11 is the ruin of every doctrine that guarantees deliverance to faith. In one sentence, men who through faith stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword and turned armies to flight; and in the next, others who were tortured, not accepting deliverance, had trial of mockings and scourgings, were stoned, sawn asunder, slain with the sword, and wandered in sheepskins. The chapter does not divide them into the faithful and the failures. It says these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise. Faith sometimes turns armies and sometimes goes into the fire, and it is the same faith.

Deuteronomy 32:30 supplies the arithmetic underneath both outcomes. If one man chases a thousand of Israel, the explanation is not the enemy's prowess but that their Rock had sold them. Israel's victories were never about numbers and neither were her defeats. Applied honestly, this cuts both ways: a church should not congratulate itself on success it did not produce, and should look first to its own faithfulness when it is scattered. And Matthew 24:20 shows how tenderly the Lord treats those who must flee — He does not promise they will not run; He tells them to pray it will not be winter.
